en: The Preface and Chapters on the Chan Gate of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, for All Sons of the Buddha to Listen with Palms Joined and a Sincere Heart. I now wish to speak the chapters on the comprehensive discourse (*sitan*) of the Mahāyāna *Laṅkāvatāra*.
As for "comprehensive discourse," it refers to the fact that the Mahāyāna was once fully expounded at Mount Laṅkā. Because...
The Master Bodhidharma arrived at the Eastern Capital from the Kingdom of Linṇi in South India during the first year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty,
bringing with him the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra.
The Tripitaka Master Bhadra respectfully consulted [the original] and translated it.
This scripture consists of five fascicles in total, forming a single work;
its characters are vast and extensive, and its meaning is difficult to comprehend.
The Upādhyāya, through his great compassion, extensively saved those in the various districts.
He was thoroughly versed in the sutras and inquired after the Way, grasping the profound essence of the teachings.
Whether in times of ultimate attainment or extreme distress, all were graced by his guidance and instruction.
Furthermore, at Haoshan, the śramaṇa Huishan translated the *Xitan Zhang*.
It extensively opens the gates of dhyāna without hindering the study of wisdom;
it does not cling to written words and is entirely rendered in the Qin vernacular.
He was well-versed in the phonology of Kumārajīva Dharma Master;
[the sounds] beginning with *lu*, *liu*, *lu*,
and *lou*, as well as *po-lo-duo* and *po-lo-duo*.
First is the seat of purity through relinquishing conditions;
all things do not arise, for there is true non-self.
Proceeding directly toward Bodhi, one is free from cause and effect.
The mind is quiescent in every thought, free from calamity;
in every moment, there is no-thought—this should be affirmed.
*Mati-li-ma-ru-lu-lu-lou-po-ra-duo*. O sons of the Buddhas, do not be indolent; exhort yourselves.
The river of craving and the sea of suffering must be crossed;
remembering food but not eating, one is constantly hungry;
if wood is not gathered, fire will not emerge.
Yelaluo sits upright; Sahaye does not lie down;
Jiling Sheng, Jiling Sheng.
In the second stage of abiding, one constantly observes purity;
yet though there is seeing and hearing, there is no actual looking or listening.
Both arising and ceasing have vanished, yet this is because [ultimate] realization has not yet been attained.
Only through the words transmitted by the teacher is meditative concentration truly revealed;
one perceives that the Buddha’s Dharmakāya is of non-dual nature.
*Svabhāva-mūrdha-pratigrahaṃ jru-lu-lu-lu-lu-ji-liṅ-śeng*. O sons of the Buddhas, do not be angry or deceitful!
When the three poisons suddenly arise, there is no Buddha-nature;
with a deluded and frantic mind in chaos, one afflicts the worthy and holy.
The eyes greedily crave the dust of forms, and the ears are bound by listening.
Turning one's back on heaven and heading toward evil paths,
one now fills the mandate by practicing meditative concentration;
may the Sahā world return to the right path.
Sā-laṅ-yǎng sā-laṅ-yǎng.
Third, in observing the mind, one must be thorough and diligent;
sweep away defilements and eliminate calamities and obstacles.
Form is itself emptiness, meeting with the absence of conceptualization;
deluded thought and discrimination are merely the measure of the mind.
Upon the essence of consciousness, the essence is truly non-existent—there is no slander.
Bāṭiri bāru lu lū lū sālaṅ. O sons of the Buddhas, do not slander!
All possess the karmic obstacles of sinful deeds;
when their families hear this sound, they will not release them.
The three-inch tongue-root creates delusion;
speaking long where it should be short, it vexes the Heart-King.
The Heart-King does not understand this speaking of long and short.
In future lives, one will suffer the calamities of the paths of karma;
therefore, the sheep and the attendants should together sweep the hall clean for a time of making offerings.
Fusuzhi, fusuzhi. The fourth [stage] unites the eighth consciousness with the sixth and seventh;
observing that the mind and its essence are fundamentally the meditation chamber.
The Dharma-body and the dharmas of the body are not one;
the five eyes, six supernormal powers, and the sun of radiant wisdom—
upon hearing these words, one immediately awakens to the fact that there is truly no secret.
Miti li mi lu liu lou fu su zhi. O sons of the Buddhas, do not be negligent!
Since beginningless time you have dwelt in a dark chamber;
wandering through the cycle of birth and death, you have been unable to emerge.
It is only because of ignorance and delusion that they obstruct the sun of wisdom. Yishumili yishumili svāhā jishi.
Xiaoliao yao xiaoliao yao.
Within the fifth gate of the true mark (dharmatā),
all fame and profit are illuminated as false invocations;
they are like breath already stilled, appearing as both form and non-form.
Neither cause nor effect, there is no anger or resentment.
Looking at the nature within the nature, it is wondrous among the wondrous.
Essential, fundamental, lu, liu, lu, lou, xiao, liao, yao—O sons of the Buddhas, do not be angry or resentful!
Sorrow, grief, anger, and resentment are obstacles to the Path.
Within this gateway of the Path, there is no anger or resentment;
one must clarify the mind and observe both the internal and external illumination.
If there is a film over the eye, it must be polished;
a copper mirror that is not polished is unfit for reflection.
From afar, one perceives things as being well-made through conjecture.
Sahaye mo nātra. Anurānta anurānta.
This is the sixth mental state: the gate of meditative concentration through contemplation of detachment.
Neither coming nor going, it has no boundaries.
Upon awakening, observe the awakening itself to eliminate both concentration and distraction.
The Buddha-son and sentient beings share the same essential substance.
The Fundamental Purity: A Discourse on the Dispelling of Defilements.
*Tirikhānulu lūlun ānrai pan*. O Sons of the Buddhas, do not look at Maṅkan.
On the path, a great rākṣasa calls out.
Fools come and go, constantly bound by fetters;
their minds are distracted and disordered by attachment to the dust of sensory forms.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they possess no stability or integrity.
He cried out recklessly amidst the assembly;
when others exhorted him, he immediately became obstinate and difficult to correct.
[The Buddha] administered the *yera-loda* (ye-rā-ro-da) medicinal wash.
Sahajeya-dunhan. Praluyu praluyu.
The seventh, the Great Wisdom of Perfect Radiance, awakens.
The eighteen categories of detachment from names through the four gates,
the subtle existence of arising and ceasing that transcends all,
and the Great Master of the triple world— truly difficult to encounter.
Birth-and-death and nirvana do not meet;
one does not linger while rowing upstream against the river of craving.
When the mind is realized as non-mind, demons depart of their own accord.
Kiṭi kiṭu kiḷu kiḷū kiḷu kiḷo kiḷe | O sons of the Buddhas, always remain awakened;
with a single thought of pure mind free from defilement,
all demonic armies will naturally depart.
The commoners repeatedly focused their attention;
Sahaja attained great enlightenment. *Sāhalaya sāhalaya*.
The eighth dhyāna-gate is beyond the piercing of needles or the pouring of liquids;
it is neither high nor low, possessing no pavilions;
it neither issues forth nor enters within, possessing no city walls.
This contemplation reveals that sound is the very beginning of learning;
when thoughts arise and the mind moves, do not allow them to become attached.
Sit for long periods and apply effort, whether in action or non-action.
That there is no pleasure to be enjoyed is the eternal pleasure.
A single illumination from the lamp of wisdom reaches the three thousand worlds;
the water of meditative concentration is eternally clear throughout the eighty-four thousand teachings.
The Buddhas of the ten directions have together opened the way to awakening.
*Joti-ri-boru-ryu-ro-ru-sa-yak*. O sons of the Buddha, act with mastery; do not be constrained.
In the four intermediate directions, above, and below, it cannot be measured;
abiding in the gate of quiescent nirvana, it is vast and expansive,
profoundly peaceful, blissful, and unattached.
The perfect awakening of Sahāya.
